title: Saloks at the close of a reading
hookLine: his saloks are read near the end of every complete reading of the Granth, often at a bhog for someone who has died

lines: A READING, FIRST PAGE TO LAST.
cards: A living room has been cleared of furniture. White sheets cover the floor.
At one end, on a raised platform under a canopy, the Guru Granth Sahib lies open, and for several days, in shifts, family and friends have been reading it aloud from the first page to the last.
A grandfather died ten days ago. Today is the last day of the reading. The house is full; someone is stirring a huge pot of karah prashad in the kitchen.
And as the reader nears the last pages, the words that fill the room are the ones we've spent this month with.

teach.h: A PATH: THE WHOLE GRANTH, READ ALOUD.
teach.b: A complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is called a path. An akhand path runs without stopping, reader after reader, from the first page to the last. A sahaj path goes at an easier pace, over days or weeks.
Either way, the reading ends with a ceremony called the bhog: the completion. Because the book has its order, every complete reading ends the same way.

teach.h: HIS SALOKS COME NEAR THE END.
teach.b: Near the very end come Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, then Guru Arjan's short Mundavani, the seal, and a last salok of his.
Some sangats also read the Raagmala; Sikhs differ on that, and the Sikh code of conduct leaves it to local custom.
Then the Anand Sahib is sung, the Ardas is said, a hukamnama, the day's word, is read, and karah prashad is shared.

teach.h: THE ROOM HEARS PASSING, THEN WHAT STAYS.
teach.b: So Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are what the room hears just before a reading closes. Families often hold a sahaj path after a death, timed so the bhog falls on the day of the final prayers.
The grieving family sits and hears: janjaal, today or tomorrow. All companions go. And then: rahio.
The holy remain. I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The words were not written as funeral texts.
They come at the end because of where they sit in the book. And in that room, they fit. They don't pretend the grandfather isn't gone.
They name the passing out loud, and then they name what stays.

how: At the bhog of an akhand or sahaj path, the reader finishes the Guru Granth Sahib with Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks and the Mundavani; Anand Sahib, Ardas, a hukamnama and karah prashad follow, and many families hold this after a death.

games.q: your friend's family is holding a sahaj path after their grandfather died. you're invited to the last day. what will you hear just before the reading closes?

a new prayer written for him.
games.why: the saloks come near the very end of the Granth, so the room hears: whatever is born will pass, and then, the Name remains.

practice: Think of someone who has died, close or not so close, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, and let their face come.
Then slowly say three of the lines we've learned, pausing after each: janjaal, today or tomorrow; rahio; nothing equals it.
You're not explaining anything, just keeping them company with the words, and if you pray, you can end with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Bhog, the completion ceremony. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks come just before it, so a grieving room hears both the passing and what stays.

carryVoice: Your line: read for the departed. The words name the passing, and then what stays. Go gently.
